paper_metadata.title: Training Quantum Self-Attention Model in Near-Term Quantum Computer

summary: The paper reports training a quantum self-attention model for binary text classification on two small datasets, MC (130 sentences) and RP (105 noun phrases), on the OriginQ 'Wukong' 72-qubit superconducting device using 28 qubits in a seven-way parallel scheme. Reported hardware results were 100.00% accuracy on MC and 83.87% on RP, with 85 s forward propagation and 270 s backward propagation per step, compared with simulator results of 100.00%/80.66% accuracy and 5567 s/9092 s timing.

experiments.description: Training and evaluating a quantum self-attention model for binary text classification on the MC and RP datasets using a real superconducting quantum computer and a simulator baseline.

algorithm.variant: quantum self-attention model for text classification
algorithm.ansatz: parameterized quantum circuits with alternating Rc and CZ layers; separate circuits Uq, Uk, Uv
algorithm.optimizer: classical optimization with parameter-shift gradients; specific optimizer not reported
algorithm.convergence_criteria: trained over epochs; no explicit stopping criterion reported

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Classical input tokens are mapped into quantum states via arctan(x) followed by Rc rotation encoding; query/key/value are produced by separate parameterized circuits
problem_formulation.objective_function: text classification loss optimized by training the quantum self-attention model

problem_instance.description: Binary text classification on two NLP datasets: MC (meaning classification) and RP (relative pronoun classification)

dataset_specification.MC: 130 sentences; 70 train, 30 validation, 30 test; 3-4 words per sentence; 17-word shared vocabulary; food vs IT classes
dataset_specification.RP: 105 noun phrases from RelPron; binary classification of subject-relative vs object-relative clauses; 15-word vocabulary

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Sentences/noun phrases tokenized into short sequences; each word represented as a vector input to the quantum self-attention model; exact preprocessing beyond tokenization not reported
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Training and validation loss/accuracy tracked over epochs; test accuracy reported for simulator and hardware

noise_model.noise_type: hardware noise on real superconducting QPU

implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Expectation values measured from quantum circuits are used to compute attention scores and softmax-weighted outputs

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: training and validation loss/accuracy curves shown over epochs; hardware slightly outperformed simulator on both datasets

speedup_claims.conditions: combining attention-level, token-level, and batch-level parallelism
speedup_claims.caveats: Claimed speedup is relative to the non-parallel strategy; depends on available qubits and parallel execution assumptions.

speedup_claims.conditions: example with average sentence length 20 tokens and batch size 16
speedup_claims.caveats: This is an illustrative calculation in the text, not an experimentally measured speedup.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Forward training time scales as O(3 * bs * n * Tanz); with parallel strategies, claimed speedup factor up to 3 * bs * n

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: 28 qubits on a 72-qubit superconducting device; 2000 shots per circuit; seven-way parallel scheme
limiting_factors: No classical algorithmic baseline beyond simulator comparison
Speedup claims are relative to a non-parallel quantum implementation, not to a classical method
Small NLP benchmark sizes (MC 130 samples, RP 105 samples)
Heavy dependence on parallel qubit availability and repeated sampling
Data loading and measurement overheads are nontrivial

notes: The paper reports experiments on the 'Wukong' 72-qubit superconducting quantum computer and states a seven-way parallel scheme using 28 qubits.
The paper also reports a simulator baseline, but the quantum experiment of interest is the real-hardware run; simulator results are treated as baseline, not a separate experiment.
Circuit depth, gate counts, and variational parameter counts are not explicitly reported in the text provided.
The paper reports better hardware than simulator results on RP and similar accuracy on MC, but does not compare against a classical NLP baseline.
The claimed 960x speedup is theoretical and relative to a non-parallel quantum strategy, not a demonstrated classical advantage.
